\chapter{The Stretches A Calendar Marks}
\label{ch:la-jornada-y-la-decada}
\hlchaptermodality{349}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name la jornada, la decada, la fiesta, el aniversario and la agenda, and say why a journey was once one day's travel.}

Complete ES-C349-agenda: name a day's stretch, a decade, a holiday and an anniversary, and name the book they are written in.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la jornada]{la jornada — a day's worth, and the journey inside it}

\label{lesson:ES-C349-jornada}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the delay}, then \emph{the turn}. (\emph{La demora}; \emph{el turno}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el día — the same Latin day, by a different road.
  \item la hora — what this is measured in.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hor-NA-da}, three beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{j} is the scraped \emph{jota}, back in the throat. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la jornada} — \textquotedblleft{}a day's stretch\textquotedblright{}: a working day, a day's march, a day's play.

Latin \textbf{diēs} was \emph{day}, and \textbf{diurnus} meant \emph{belonging to the day}. Spanish already had \emph{día} straight from \emph{diēs}. So why a second word?

Because this one came the long way round. \textbf{Diurnāta} travelled north into Occitan and French, was reshaped there into \textbf{jornada} and \textbf{journée}, and then walked back south into Spanish as a borrowing. Two words, one Latin day, different roads — which is why they do not look alike.

The northern road left tracks in English. A \textbf{journey} was originally \emph{one day's travel}. A \textbf{journal} is a \emph{day-book}. To \textbf{adjourn} is to put something off to \emph{another day}, and a \textbf{sojourn} is a stay counted in days. \textbf{Diurnal} came by the straight Latin route.

\emph{Jornada} is the word a Spanish speaker reaches for when a day is a quantity of work rather than a square on a calendar.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A day measured by what fits inside it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la jornada}
  \item \emph{una jornada de ocho horas}
  \item \emph{la jornada de hoy}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \textbf{journey} at first? (One day's travel.) And which Spanish word comes from the same \emph{diēs} by the straight road? (\emph{Día}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la década]{la década — ten years, and the ten scattered through English}

\label{lesson:ES-C349-decada}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the turn}, then \emph{a day's stretch}. (\emph{El turno}; \emph{la jornada}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez — the ten this counts by.
  \item veinte — two of them.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{DÉ-ca-da}, three beats with the weight on the first, which is why it is written with an accent. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la década} — \textquotedblleft{}the decade,\textquotedblright{} ten years taken as one block.

Greek \textbf{déka} is \emph{ten}. A \textbf{dekás} was \emph{a set of ten} — of soldiers, of verses, of anything. Latin borrowed it as \textbf{decas}, and Spanish as \textbf{década}.

Latin also had its own \emph{ten}, \textbf{decem}, and the two roots are the same ancient word travelling by different families. Between them they seeded English thickly.

\textbf{Decimal} counts by tens. To \textbf{decimate} a legion was to execute one man in ten. A \textbf{dime} is a tenth of a dollar. And \textbf{December} is the \emph{tenth} month — which it was, before Rome shoved January and February in front of it and left the last four months carrying the wrong numbers forever.

Even a \textbf{dean} is here: a \emph{decanus} was a man set over ten monks.

Spanish keeps it as well, in the \emph{diez} you already count with.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Time in blocks bigger than a day.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la década}
  \item \emph{una década}
  \item \emph{en una década}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What number is \emph{déka}? (Ten.) And why is \textbf{December} named for the tenth? (It was the tenth month before January and February were added.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la fiesta]{la fiesta — the day set apart, and the word English took twice}

\label{lesson:ES-C349-fiesta}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a day's stretch}, then \emph{a decade}. (\emph{La jornada}; \emph{la década}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item feliz — how the day is meant to feel.
  \item la semana — the run of days it interrupts.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{FIES-ta}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{ie} is one glide, not two beats. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la fiesta} — \textquotedblleft{}the holiday,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}the party.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{fēstus} meant \emph{set apart, solemn, not for work}. A \textbf{fēstum} was such a day, and the plural \textbf{fēsta} — the feast days — is what Spanish inherited, which is why the word arrives already meaning a whole stretch rather than a single hour.

That double sense is still there. \emph{La fiesta} can be a public holiday marked on a calendar, or the party you throw on a Saturday night, and Spanish does not think it needs two words.

English took the Latin road first and got \textbf{feast}, \textbf{festival}, \textbf{festive}, \textbf{festoon} and \textbf{fête}. Then, much later, it borrowed the Spanish shape whole, so \textbf{fiesta} now sits in an English dictionary beside \textbf{feast}, the same word arriving twice, centuries apart, by different ships.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The days a calendar marks off from the rest.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la fiesta}
  \item \emph{una fiesta grande}
  \item \emph{el día de la fiesta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{fēstus} mean? (Set apart, not for work.) And which plain English word is the same Latin word? (Feast.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el aniversario]{el aniversario — the year turning back to the same day}

\label{lesson:ES-C349-aniversario}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a decade}, then \emph{the holiday}. (\emph{La década}; \emph{la fiesta}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ¿Cuántos años tienes? — the year this counts.
  \item los meses — the twelve it walks through.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-ni-ver-SA-rio}, five beats with the weight on the fourth. The \emph{v} is made with both lips, close to a soft \emph{b}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el aniversario} — \textquotedblleft{}the anniversary.\textquotedblright{}

Two Latin pieces. \textbf{Annus} is \emph{a year}. \textbf{Vertere} is \emph{to turn}. Put them together and \textbf{anniversārius} means \emph{the year-turning} — the wheel has gone all the way round and stopped where it started.

That is a more exact picture than the English feeling of the word. An anniversary is not a memory. It is a position: the year has come back to the same mark.

\textbf{Annus} gave English \textbf{annual}, \textbf{annals} (a year-by-year record), \textbf{biennial} and \textbf{per annum}.

\textbf{Vertere} is even busier. A \textbf{verse} is where the plough turns at the end of a furrow. To \textbf{convert} is to turn something round; to \textbf{reverse} is to turn it back. \textbf{Versus} sets one side turned against another, and \textbf{vertigo} is the world turning when it should not.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A date that comes back around, and a reason to call it a \emph{fiesta}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el aniversario}
  \item \emph{un aniversario feliz}
  \item \emph{el aniversario es hoy}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two Latin words are inside it? (\emph{Annus}, year, and \emph{vertere}, to turn.) And what does \textbf{vertigo} name? (The world turning when it should not.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la agenda]{la agenda — the things that must be done}

\label{lesson:ES-C349-agenda}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the holiday}, then \emph{the anniversary}. (\emph{La fiesta}; \emph{el aniversario}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la semana — what it is usually laid out by.
  \item los meses — the bigger squares in it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-JEN-da}, three beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{g} before \emph{e} is the scraped \emph{jota}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la agenda} — \textquotedblleft{}the diary,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the schedule,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the list of what is coming.\textquotedblright{}

This one is a Latin grammatical form that walked into modern life without being translated. \textbf{Agenda} is a plural, and it means \emph{the things that must be done}. Not things done, not things happening — things owed to the future.

Behind it stands \textbf{agere}, one of Latin's great workhorse verbs. Its first sense is to \textbf{drive}, the way a herdsman drives cattle down a road.

Once you know the driving is there, the family opens up. An \textbf{agent} is somebody who drives a thing along. Something \textbf{agile} moves quickly. \textbf{Agitate} is to drive hard and repeatedly. To \textbf{act} is \emph{agere} itself, and so are \textbf{exact}, \textbf{transact} and \textbf{navigate}.

And an \emph{agenda} is the herd of tasks being driven at you.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five stretches of time and the book you write them in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la agenda}
  \item \emph{mi agenda}
  \item \emph{la agenda de la semana}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{agenda} mean, word for word? (The things that must be done.) And what does \textbf{agere} mean first of all? (To drive, as a herdsman drives cattle.)
\end{tcolorbox}
